hand/anabelian-geometry.html:
The Grothendieck–Teichmüller Group and Outer Galois Actions

The Grothendieck–Teichmüller group, denoted GT, was introduced by Drinfeld in 1990 as a profinite group that acts on the tower of profinite completions of mapping class groups of punctured spheres. It sits in a short exact sequence 1 → GT → Out(π₁(ℙ¹{0,1,∞})) → Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ) → 1, where the outer automorphism group of the étale fundamental group of the thrice‑punctured projective line receives the natural Galois action. Ihara showed that the absolute Galois group G_ℚ embeds into GT via the cyclotomic character and the action on torsion points of the Tate module of the multiplicative group. This embedding is conjectured to be an isomorphism after passing to the pro‑ℓ completion for each prime ℓ, a statement known as the Grothendieck–Teichmüller conjecture. The group GT also controls the deformation theory of associators in the sense of Drinfeld, linking anabelian geometry to quantum groups and the theory of motives. In practical terms, any isomorphism of étale fundamental groups of hyperbolic curves over number fields that respects the outer Galois action must arise from an element of GT. This makes GT the natural symmetry group of the anabelian reconstruction problem: two curves with isomorphic fundamental groups as G_K-modules are isomorphic if and only if the isomorphism lies in the image of GT. Recent work by Schneps, Lochak, and others has computed the Lie algebra of GT in terms of multiple zeta values, providing explicit generators and relations that can be used to test the conjecture in low‑weight cases.

p-Adic Anabelian Geometry and the Reconstruction of Hyperbolic Curves

When the base field K is a finite extension of ℚ_p, the étale fundamental group π₁(X) of a smooth hyperbolic curve X/K carries a rich p‑adic Hodge‑theoretic structure. Mochizuki proved the p‑adic Grothendieck conjecture (1999): for hyperbolic curves X, Y over a p‑adic field, the natural map Isom_K(X,Y) → IsomG_K(π₁(XK̄), π₁(YK̄))/π₁(Y) is a bijection. The proof uses the theory of indigenous bundles — certain filtered vector bundles with integrable connection on the curve — together with the p‑adic Simpson correspondence to reconstruct the curve from its fundamental group. A key ingredient is the p‑adic monodromy theorem of Fontaine, which identifies the Galois representation on the Tate module of the Jacobian with a filtered (φ, Γ)-module. The decomposition groups at primes of K correspond to inertia subgroups in π₁(X), and the local reciprocity law identifies the abelianized inertia with the multiplicative group of the completion. By analysing the filtration on the de Rham cohomology of the universal cover, one recovers the Hodge filtration on H¹dR(X/K), which determines the curve up to isomorphism via the Torelli theorem. The p‑adic theory also yields a version of the section conjecture for local fields: a section of 1 → π₁(XK̄) → π₁(X) → G_K → 1 corresponds to a K-rational point if and only if it respects the Hodge‑Tate weights of the associated Galois representation. This result has been extended by Tamagawa and others to the case of semi‑stable reduction, where the fundamental group is replaced by the log‑étale fundamental group of a proper model.

Worked Example: p‑Adic Reconstruction
Let K = ℚ_p and let X be the modular curve X₁(p) over K. Suppose an isomorphism φ : π₁(XK̄) → π₁(YK̄) of profinite groups commutes with the outer G_K-action. Explain why φ must come from a unique K-isomorphism X ≅ Y.
By Mochizuki's p‑adic Grothendieck conjecture, the functor X ↦ π₁(X) from hyperbolic curves over K to profinite groups equipped with a continuous outer G_K-action is fully faithful. The hypothesis that φ respects the outer action means it is a morphism in the target category. Full faithfulness gives a unique isomorphism f : X → Y inducing φ on fundamental groups. The proof uses indigenous bundles to reconstruct the Hodge filtration on H¹dR and then applies the Torelli theorem for curves with level structure.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about reconstruction over p‑adic fields, immediately recall the three pillars: (1) indigenous bundles and the p‑adic Simpson correspondence, (2) the p‑adic monodromy theorem linking Galois representations to filtered (φ, Γ)-modules, (3) the Torelli step that passes from Hodge filtration to the curve. Mentioning these by name earns full credit even if the proof details are omitted.

Birational Anabelian Geometry: Function Fields and Pseudo‑Galois Covers

The birational version of the Grothendieck conjecture replaces the base number field by a finitely generated extension K/k of a perfect field k. Pop and Koenigsmann proved (2000s) that for smooth hyperbolic curves X, Y over K, the natural map Isom_K(X,Y) → IsomG_K(π₁(XK̄), π₁(YK̄))/π₁(Y) is a bijection. Their method introduces pseudo‑Galois covers: finite étale covers Z → X whose Galois closure has group a projective profinite group. By analysing the lattice of such covers inside the fundamental group, one recovers the function field K(X) as the fixed field of the kernel of the outer action on the set of decomposition groups. The key technical tool is the Neukirch–Uchida theorem for function fields, which identifies the absolute Galois group of a finitely generated field with its profinite completion. This allows one to translate group‑theoretic data (open subgroups, normalizers, centralizers) back into field‑theoretic data (subfields, valuations). The birational section conjecture, also proved by Koenigsmann, states that sections of 1 → π₁(XK̄) → π₁(X) → G_K → 1 correspond bijectively to K-rational points of X. The proof uses the fact that a section determines a compatible system of decomposition groups, which in turn defines a valuation on K(X) trivial on K; the valuation ring is a discrete valuation ring with residue field K, giving a rational point. This birational theory is the only setting where the full section conjecture is currently a theorem.

Indigenous Bundles, Hodge Monodromy, and Mochizuki's Proof of the Curve Conjecture

Mochizuki's proof of the Grothendieck conjecture for curves over number fields (1996) rests on the theory of indigenous bundles. An indigenous bundle on a hyperbolic curve X is a pair (E, ∇) where E is a vector bundle of rank two with trivial determinant and ∇ is a logarithmic connection whose residues at the cusps lie in a prescribed set of nilpotent matrices. The moduli space of indigenous bundles is a torsor under the additive group of quadratic differentials, and its fundamental group is canonically isomorphic to π₁(X). The Hodge‑theoretic monodromy arises from the variation of Hodge structure on the de Rham cohomology of the universal indigenous bundle; this monodromy representation factors through the outer action of G_K on π₁(X). By comparing the Hodge filtration on the de Rham realization with the weight filtration on the ℓ‑adic étale cohomology (via the p‑adic comparison isomorphisms of Faltings), one reconstructs the Hodge filtration on H¹dR(X/K). The Torelli theorem for curves with level structure then yields the isomorphism class of X. The proof also uses the rigid analytic uniformization of X by the Drinfeld upper half‑plane, which identifies the étale fundamental group with a Schottky group. The indigenous bundle construction is functorial with respect to isomorphisms of fundamental groups, so any G_K-equivariant isomorphism π₁(X) ≅ π₁(Y) induces an isomorphism of the corresponding moduli spaces of indigenous bundles, hence an isomorphism of the underlying curves.

Higher‑Dimensional Anabelian Problems: Abelian Varieties and K3 Surfaces

Anabelian geometry beyond curves is largely conjectural. For an abelian variety A over a number field K, the étale fundamental group is the profinite completion of the Tate module T_ℓ(A) (a free ℤ_ℓ-module of rank 2 dim A) together with the Galois action. The Tate conjecture predicts that the Galois representation on T_ℓ(A) determines A up to isogeny; Faltings proved this for abelian varieties over number fields (1983). However, the full anabelian statement — that π₁(A) as a G_K-module determines A up to isomorphism — remains open because the polarization data is not visible in the fundamental group alone. For K3 surfaces, the étale fundamental group is trivial (simply connected), so the anabelian philosophy must be reformulated using the geometric fundamental group of a suitable open subset or the Brauer group with its Galois action. Recent work by Esnault–Kerlo and others studies the anabelian properties of the moduli space of polarized K3 surfaces, where the fundamental group is the mapping class group of the K3 lattice. The section conjecture for higher‑dimensional varieties would involve sections of 1 → π₁(XK̄) → π₁(X) → G_K → 1 for smooth projective X with ample canonical bundle; no general results are known beyond curves. The main obstruction is the lack of a higher‑dimensional analogue of the Torelli theorem that is functorial with respect to fundamental group isomorphisms.

  • Confusing the Grothendieck–Teichmüller group with the absolute Galois group; they are related but not equal.
  • Assuming the p‑adic Grothendieck conjecture holds for all varieties; it is proved only for hyperbolic curves.
  • Overlooking the role of indigenous bundles in Mochizuki's proof; they are the bridge between fundamental groups and Hodge theory.
  • Treating the birational section conjecture as equivalent to the number‑field version; the former is a theorem, the latter is open.
  • Believing that abelian varieties are anabelian in the same sense as curves; their fundamental groups are abelian and lose polarization data.
  • Neglecting the distinction between étale and log‑étale fundamental groups when reduction is not smooth.
  • Remember that the anabelian reconstruction for higher‑dimensional varieties remains conjectural and no general theorem exists.

hand/integrable-systems.html:
The Inverse Scattering Transform for the Schrödinger Operator

The inverse scattering transform (IST) for the Korteweg–de Vries equation is built on the spectral theory of the one‑dimensional Schrödinger operator L = −∂ₓ² + u(x). For a potential u(x) that decays sufficiently fast as |x| → ∞, the continuous spectrum covers λ ≥ 0 and there may be a finite number of negative eigenvalues λ = −κⱼ² (κⱼ > 0) corresponding to bound states. The direct scattering problem constructs the scattering data: the reflection coefficient R(k) for k ∈ ℝ (where λ = k²), the discrete eigenvalues −κⱼ², and the norming constants cⱼ defined by the asymptotic behaviour of the Jost solutions. The Jost solutions f±(x,k) satisfy f±(x,k) ∼ e±ikx as x → ±∞. The transmission coefficient T(k) and reflection coefficients R±(k) are defined by the linear relations between f+ and f−. For the KdV equation uₜ − 6uuₓ + uₓₓₓ = 0, the potential evolves according to u(x,t) and the scattering data evolve linearly: R(k,t) = R(k,0)e8ik³t, κⱼ(t) = κⱼ(0), cⱼ(t) = cⱼ(0)e8κⱼ³t. The inverse problem reconstructs u(x,t) from the time‑dependent scattering data via the Gel'fand–Levitan–Marchenko integral equation. For reflectionless potentials (R(k) ≡ 0) the Marchenko equation degenerates to a linear algebraic system, yielding the N‑soliton solution. The one‑soliton solution is u(x,t) = 2κ² sech²[κ(x − 4κ²t − x₀)], where κ and x₀ are determined by the single bound state and its norming constant. The multi‑soliton solution exhibits elastic collisions: after interaction each soliton retains its shape and velocity, acquiring only a phase shift. The IST thus linearises the KdV flow on the nonlinear Fourier space of scattering data.

The AKNS Hierarchy and the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation

The Ablowitz–Kaup–Newell–Segur (AKNS) scheme provides a unified Lax pair formulation for a large family of integrable equations, including the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation, the modified KdV (mKdV) equation, and the sine‑Gordon equation. The AKNS Lax pair consists of two 2×2 matrix operators depending on a spectral parameter λ: L = i∂ₓ + Q(x,t,λ) and M = i∂ₜ + V(x,t,λ), where Q = [[0, q], [r, 0]] and V is a polynomial in λ with coefficients built from q, r and their derivatives. The zero‑curvature condition Lₜ − Mₓ + [L, M] = 0 generates an infinite hierarchy of evolution equations for the potentials q(x,t) and r(x,t). Choosing V as a quadratic polynomial in λ yields the NLS system: iqₜ + qₓₓ + 2q²r = 0, −irₜ + rₓₓ + 2qr² = 0. With the reduction r = ∓q* one obtains the focusing/defocusing NLS equation iqₜ + qₓₓ ± 2|q|²q = 0. The AKNS hierarchy also contains the mKdV equation via the reduction r = q, and the sine‑Gordon equation via a different reduction and a spectral parameter dependent gauge transformation. The inverse scattering transform for the AKNS system is developed by analysing the Jost solutions of the first‑order system Ψₓ = (iλσ₃ + Q)Ψ, where σ₃ = diag(1,−1). The scattering matrix S(λ) relates the Jost solutions at ±∞ and its entries evolve linearly in time. The reconstruction of q and r from the scattering data is achieved through a Riemann–Hilbert problem or a system of singular integral equations. The AKNS formalism demonstrates that the NLS equation is a completely integrable Hamiltonian system with an infinite sequence of conserved quantities generated by the expansion of log a(λ), where a(λ) is the transmission coefficient. The soliton solutions of NLS are obtained from the discrete eigenvalues of the scattering problem; the one‑soliton solution of the focusing NLS is q(x,t) = 2η sech[2η(x − 2ξt − x₀)] ei(2ξx + 2(η²−ξ²)t + φ₀), where λ = ξ + iη is the eigenvalue in the upper half‑plane.

Worked Example: One‑Soliton Solution of the Focusing NLS via IST
Given the scattering data for the focusing NLS equation iqₜ + qₓₓ + 2|q|²q = 0 consisting of a single discrete eigenvalue λ₁ = iη (η > 0) with norming constant C₁ = 2η e2iηx₀, and zero reflection coefficient, reconstruct the one‑soliton solution q(x,t).
For the AKNS system with r = −q*, the time evolution of the norming constant is C₁(t) = C₁(0) e4iλ₁²t. With λ₁ = iη, λ₁² = −η², so C₁(t) = 2η e2iηx₀ e−4iη²t. The inverse problem for a single pole in the upper half‑plane yields the solution q(x,t) = 2η sech[2η(x − x₀ − 4η²t)] ei(2η²t + φ₀) after adjusting the phase. More precisely, the standard formula gives q(x,t) = 2η sech[2η(x − 2ξt − x₀)] ei(2ξx + 2(η²−ξ²)t + φ₀) with ξ = 0. Hence q(x,t) = 2η sech[2η(x − x₀)] ei(2η²t + φ₀). The norming constant phase determines φ₀; matching the asymptotic phase yields φ₀ = 0. Thus the one‑soliton solution is q(x,t) = 2η sech[2η(x − x₀)] e2iη²t.
Exam Strategy: Recognising AKNS Reductions
When a question asks to identify the integrable equation from a given Lax pair, check the structure of Q and the degree of V in λ. The AKNS Lax pair with Q = [[0, q], [r, 0]] and V quadratic in λ produces the NLS system. If r = q, the system reduces to mKdV; if r = −q*, it gives the focusing/defocusing NLS. Memorise these reductions and the corresponding dispersion relations to quickly match equations to their Lax representations.

Bi‑Hamiltonian Structures and Recursion Operators

Many integrable PDEs possess two compatible Hamiltonian structures, a property known as bi‑Hamiltonianity. For the KdV equation uₜ = uₓₓₓ − 6uuₓ, the first Hamiltonian structure is given by the Poisson operator J₁ = ∂ₓ with Hamiltonian H₁ = ∫ (uₓ²/2 + u³) dx, so that uₜ = J₁ δH₁/δu. The second Hamiltonian structure uses the operator J₂ = ∂ₓ³ + 2u∂ₓ + uₓ with Hamiltonian H₀ = ∫ u²/2 dx, yielding the same equation: uₜ = J₂ δH₀/δu. The two Poisson operators are compatible, meaning any linear combination J₂ + λJ₁ is also a Poisson operator. Magri's theorem states that if a system is bi‑Hamiltonian with compatible Poisson structures, it possesses an infinite hierarchy of commuting flows and conserved quantities. The recursion operator R = J₂ J₁⁻¹ = ∂ₓ² + 2u + 2uₓ∂ₓ⁻¹ generates the hierarchy: starting from the seed symmetry uₓ = R⁰ uₓ, successive applications produce higher symmetries uₜₙ = Rⁿ uₓ. For KdV, R maps the x‑translation symmetry to the KdV flow, then to the fifth‑order flow, etc. The conserved densities are obtained from the expansion of the fractional power of R or from the Lenard–Magri scheme: J₁ δHₙ₊₁/δu = J₂ δHₙ/δu. The recursion operator is a pseudo‑differential operator; its formal inverse involves the nonlocal operator ∂ₓ⁻¹. The existence of a hereditary recursion operator (satisfying a certain Nijenhuis torsion condition) guarantees the involutivity of the generated conserved quantities. Bi‑Hamiltonian structures also underlie the Hamiltonian formulation of the KP hierarchy and the AKNS system, where the recursion operator is built from the Lax matrix.

The Painlevé Test for Integrable Partial Differential Equations

The Painlevé property — that all movable singularities of solutions are poles — serves as a powerful integrability criterion for nonlinear PDEs. The Weiss–Tabor–Carnevale (WTC) algorithm extends the Painlevé test to PDEs by seeking a Laurent‑type expansion around a non‑characteristic movable singularity manifold φ(x,t) = 0. For an equation of order m, one substitutes u = φ^α Σj=0^∞ u_j φ^j, where α is a negative integer (the leading order). The resonances (values of j where arbitrary functions enter) are found by linearising the recursion at the leading order. The equation passes the Painlevé test if all resonances are integers, the leading order is consistent, and the compatibility conditions at each resonance are satisfied identically (i.e., no extra constraints on the arbitrary functions). For the KdV equation uₜ + uₓₓₓ − 6uuₓ = 0, the leading order is α = −2 with u₀ = 2φₓ². The resonances are j = −1, 4, 6. The resonance j = −1 corresponds to the arbitrariness of the manifold φ; the resonances j = 4 and 6 must be checked for compatibility. The KdV equation passes the test, confirming its integrability. The KP equation (uₜ + 6uuₓ − uₓₓₓ)ₓ + 3uᵧᵧ = 0 also passes with leading order α = −2 and resonances −1, 4, 5, 6. The Painlevé test can also be used to discover new integrable equations by imposing the Painlevé property on a parameterised family of PDEs. However, the test is not a rigorous proof of integrability; there exist equations with the Painlevé property that are not integrable in the sense of having a Lax pair or infinite conservation laws. Conversely, some integrable systems (e.g., certain reductions of the KP hierarchy) may fail the standard WTC test but pass a modified version allowing fractional powers or logarithmic terms. The Painlevé analysis remains a standard first check for integrability in applied mathematics and mathematical physics.

Finite‑Gap Integration and Theta‑Functional Solutions

Finite‑gap (or algebro‑geometric) solutions of the KdV equation are quasi‑periodic solutions associated with a hyperelliptic Riemann surface of genus g. The spectral problem −ψₓₓ + uψ = λψ with a periodic potential u(x+L) = u(x) leads to a Floquet–Bloch spectrum consisting of bands separated by gaps. A finite‑gap potential is one for which the spectrum has only finitely many gaps; the number of gaps equals the genus g of the associated Riemann surface Γ defined by μ² = ∏j=02g (λ − Eⱼ), where Eⱼ are the band edges. The potential is reconstructed from the Baker–Akhiezer function ψ(P,x,t), a meromorphic function on Γ with an essential singularity at the point at infinity, satisfying the auxiliary linear problems. The KdV potential is given by u(x,t) = 2∂ₓ² log θ(Ux + Vt + Z₀) + constant, where θ is the Riemann theta function on the Jacobian of Γ, U and V are vectors of periods of certain meromorphic differentials, and Z₀ is a constant vector determined by the initial divisor of poles of ψ. The theta function is defined as θ(z|B) = Σn∈ℤ^g exp(πi nᵀ B n + 2πi nᵀ z), where B is the period matrix of Γ. For g = 1, the theta function reduces to the Jacobi theta function and the solution is the cnoidal wave u(x,t) = 2k² cn²(√(E₁−E₃) x − ...) + constant. For g = 2, the solution is a two‑phase quasi‑periodic wave. The finite‑gap construction provides explicit formulas for all conserved quantities and action‑angle variables: the actions are the gap lengths, and the angles are the linear flows on the Jacobian. The Krichever correspondence extends this to the KP hierarchy, where the spectral curve is an arbitrary algebraic curve with a marked point and local coordinate. Theta‑functional solutions are dense in the space of all smooth periodic solutions, and the inverse spectral transform for periodic potentials maps the potential to the spectral curve and a divisor, linearising the flow on the Jacobian.

  • Confusing the AKNS Lax pair for NLS with the Zakharov–Shabat Lax pair for the same equation; they are equivalent but differ by a gauge transformation.
  • Assuming that the recursion operator R = J₂J₁⁻¹ is always a differential operator; it is generally a pseudo‑differential operator containing ∂ₓ⁻¹ terms.
  • Misidentifying the leading order in the Painlevé test: for KdV it is −2, but for mKdV it is −1, and for the sine‑Gordon equation it is 0 (logarithmic singularity).
  • Thinking that all solutions of the KP hierarchy are given by Riemann theta functions; rational and soliton solutions correspond to degenerate curves where the theta function reduces to polynomials or exponentials.
  • Overlooking the compatibility condition at resonance j = 4 in the KdV Painlevé test; it is satisfied identically only because of the specific coefficient 6 in front of uuₓ.
  • Believing that the bi‑Hamiltonian structure of KdV is unique; there exist infinitely many compatible Poisson structures generated by the recursion operator.
  • Neglecting the role of the norming constant phase in the IST for NLS; it determines the soliton's initial position and phase, and its time evolution gives the frequency shift.

hand/chemical-thermodynamics.html:
Temperature Dependence of Enthalpy and Heat Capacities

The enthalpy change of a reaction is not strictly constant with temperature; it varies according to the difference in heat capacities between products and reactants. Kirchhoff’s law expresses this relationship as ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ∫T₁T₂ ΔCp dT, where ΔCp = Σ ν Cp(products) − Σ ν Cp(reactants). For most condensed‑phase reactions ΔCp is small, so ΔH is nearly temperature‑independent over modest ranges. In gas‑phase reactions, however, the change in the number of moles of gas can make ΔCp appreciable, and the integral must be evaluated using temperature‑dependent heat‑capacity polynomials (often of the form Cp = a + bT + cT²). Standard thermodynamic tables provide coefficients for the Shomate or NASA polynomial forms, allowing accurate ΔH values at any temperature up to several thousand kelvin. The same formalism applies to entropy: ΔS(T₂) = ΔS(T₁) + ∫T₁T₂ (ΔCp/T) dT. Because the integrand contains 1/T, entropy is more sensitive to temperature than enthalpy. In practice, examiners often ask for ΔG at a non‑standard temperature; the correct route is to compute ΔH(T) and ΔS(T) via Kirchhoff’s law and then combine them in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A common shortcut — assuming ΔH and ΔS are constant — is only justified when ΔCp ≈ 0 or when the temperature interval is narrow (≤ 50 K).

Practical Calculation Steps

  1. Obtain standard ΔH°298 and ΔS°298 from formation data.
  2. Collect Cp(T) coefficients for each species.
  3. Form ΔCp(T) = Σ ν Cp,prod(T) − Σ ν Cp,react(T).
  4. Integrate ΔCp and ΔCp/T analytically using the polynomial coefficients.
  5. Add the integrals to the 298 K values to get ΔH(T) and ΔS(T).
  6. Calculate ΔG(T) = ΔH(T) − T·ΔS(T).

When only constant‑pressure heat capacities are given, the integrals reduce to ΔCp(T₂−T₁) and ΔCp ln(T₂/T₁) respectively. This simplification is frequently used in multiple‑choice questions where the temperature shift is modest.

Third Law of Thermodynamics and Absolute Entropy

The third law states that the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is zero. This provides an absolute reference for entropy, unlike enthalpy or Gibbs energy which are defined only relative to a chosen zero. Consequently, standard molar entropies S° listed in data tables are absolute values, not formation quantities. The law also implies that it is impossible to reach 0 K by any finite number of processes, a point that occasionally appears in conceptual questions about unattainability of absolute zero. For real substances, residual entropy can arise from configurational disorder that persists at 0 K (e.g., CO crystals with random CO/OC orientations, or ice with proton disorder). Such residual entropy is measurable and must be added to the calculated lattice‑vibrational entropy to match experimental S° values. The statistical expression S = k ln W underpins this: at 0 K a perfect crystal has W = 1, giving S = 0; any degeneracy (W > 1) yields a non‑zero residual entropy. In examinations, you may be asked to estimate the residual entropy of a mole of a substance with two equally probable orientations per molecule: Sres = R ln 2 ≈ 5.76 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The third law also justifies the use of standard entropies in the reaction entropy formula ΔS°rxn = Σ ν S°(products) − Σ ν S°(reactants) without any arbitrary reference. When combining the third law with the second law, the total entropy change of the universe for a process at constant T and P can be written as ΔSuniv = −ΔG/T, linking the absolute entropy scale directly to the spontaneity criterion.

Worked Example: ΔG at 500 K from Heat‑Capacity Data
For the reaction N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g), the following data are given at 298 K: ΔH° = −92.2 kJ, ΔS° = −198.3 J K⁻¹. Constant‑pressure heat capacities (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) are: Cp(N₂) = 29.1, Cp(H₂) = 28.8, Cp(NH₃) = 35.1. Assuming Cp values are temperature‑independent, calculate ΔG at 500 K.
Step 1: ΔCp = 2(35.1) − [29.1 + 3(28.8)] = 70.2 − 115.5 = −45.3 J K⁻¹.
Step 2: ΔH(500) = ΔH(298) + ΔCp(500−298) = −92.2 kJ + (−0.0453 kJ K⁻¹)(202 K) = −92.2 − 9.15 = −101.35 kJ.
Step 3: ΔS(500) = ΔS(298) + ΔCp ln(500/298) = −198.3 J K⁻¹ + (−45.3) ln(1.677) = −198.3 − 45.3(0.517) = −198.3 − 23.4 = −221.7 J K⁻¹.
Step 4: ΔG(500) = ΔH(500) − 500·ΔS(500) = −101.35 kJ − 500(−0.2217 kJ K⁻¹) = −101.35 + 110.85 = +9.5 kJ.
Result: ΔG(500 K) ≈ +9.5 kJ, indicating the reaction is non‑spontaneous at 500 K under standard pressures.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question supplies constant Cp values, always compute ΔCp first. Use the simplified Kirchhoff integrals ΔH₂ = ΔH₁ + ΔCp(T₂−T₁) and ΔS₂ = ΔS₁ + ΔCp ln(T₂/T₁). Keep units consistent (kJ for enthalpy, J for entropy) and convert before the final ΔG = ΔH − TΔS step. A quick sanity check: if ΔCp is negative, ΔH becomes more exothermic and ΔS more negative as temperature rises; the sign of ΔG may flip, which is a favourite examiner twist.

Non‑Standard Conditions: Reaction Quotient and ΔG

The standard Gibbs energy ΔG° applies only when all reactants and products are at unit activity (1 bar for gases, 1 M for solutes, pure solids/liquids). Under real conditions the instantaneous Gibbs energy change is ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient constructed from activities. For gases, activity ≈ fugacity/1 bar; at moderate pressures fugacity ≈ pressure, so Q uses partial pressures in bar. For solutes, activity ≈ concentration/1 M (or molality/1 mol kg⁻¹) multiplied by an activity coefficient γ. In dilute solutions γ ≈ 1, but at higher ionic strengths the Debye–Hückel or extended models must be used. The sign of ΔG determines the direction of spontaneous change: ΔG < 0 → forward reaction proceeds; ΔG > 0 → reverse reaction proceeds; ΔG = 0 → equilibrium (Q = K). This relationship is the bridge between thermodynamics and chemical equilibrium. A frequent exam task is to calculate the Gibbs energy change for a given set of partial pressures or concentrations and then decide whether the system will shift toward products or reactants. Another twist: given ΔG at a non‑standard state, back‑calculate Q or an unknown partial pressure. Because ΔG° = −RT ln K, the equation can also be written as ΔG = RT ln(Q/K), which makes the comparison with the equilibrium constant explicit. When temperature changes, both ΔG° and K change according to the van’t Hoff equation, but the form ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q remains valid at each temperature.

Activity of Pure Phases

Pure solids and pure liquids have unit activity by convention, so they do not appear in Q. This simplification is crucial for heterogeneous equilibria such as CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), where Q = p(CO₂)/1 bar. The equilibrium constant Kp equals the equilibrium pressure of CO₂. In problems involving aqueous ions, the ionic strength correction often appears: log γ = −A z² √I / (1 + Ba√I). Examiners may provide A, B, a, and I, expecting you to compute γ and then the activity a = γ·c. Remember that the standard state for solutes is 1 M (or 1 mol kg⁻¹), so the numerical value of concentration in mol L⁻¹ is directly used when γ = 1.

Electrochemical Thermodynamics: ΔG and Cell Potential

Electrochemical cells provide a direct experimental route to Gibbs energy changes. For a galvanic cell the electrical work obtainable is welec = −nFEcell, where n is the number of moles of electrons transferred, F = 96485 C mol⁻¹ is Faraday’s constant, and Ecell is the cell potential. At constant T and P, the maximum non‑expansion work equals the decrease in Gibbs energy: ΔG = −nFEcell. Under standard conditions this becomes ΔG° = −nFE°cell. The Nernst equation, E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, is the electrochemical analogue of ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. It allows calculation of cell potential at any composition. A common examination question gives half‑reaction standard potentials and asks for the equilibrium constant of the overall redox reaction; the route is ΔG° = −nFE°cell followed by ΔG° = −RT ln K. Conversely, given K, one can find E°cell = (RT/nF) ln K. Temperature dependence of E° is obtained from the Gibbs‑Helmholtz relation: (∂(ΔG/T)/∂T)P = −ΔH/T², which translates to (∂E°/∂T)P = ΔS/nF. Thus a measurement of E° at two temperatures yields ΔS and ΔH for the cell reaction. In concentration cells (identical electrodes, different ion activities), E° = 0 and the potential arises solely from the activity ratio: E = (RT/nF) ln(a₂/a₁). This principle underlies ion‑selective electrodes and pH meters. Examiners often test the sign conventions: a positive Ecell corresponds to a spontaneous reaction (ΔG < 0) and a positive ΔG° corresponds to a non‑spontaneous standard reaction (E° < 0).

Thermodynamics of Solutions: Partial Molar Quantities and Activity

In multicomponent systems the extensive thermodynamic properties (G, H, S, V) are not simply additive over components because of intermolecular interactions. The partial molar Gibbs energy of component i is defined as μi = (∂G/∂ni)T,P,nj≠i, and it equals the chemical potential. For an ideal solution, μi = μi° + RT ln xi, where xi is the mole fraction and μi° is the standard chemical potential of pure i at the same T and P. Real solutions deviate; the activity ai = γi xi replaces xi, with γi the activity coefficient. The Gibbs‑Duhem equation, Σ ni dμi = 0 (at constant T, P), links the variations of chemical potentials and is the basis for determining activity coefficients from vapour‑pressure or osmotic‑pressure data. For electrolyte solutions, the mean ionic activity a± = (a+ν+ a−ν−)1/(ν+ + ν−) is used, and the Debye–Hückel limiting law gives log γ± = −A|z+z−|√I. At higher concentrations the extended Debye–Hückel or Pitzer equations are required. The concept of excess Gibbs energy GE = G − Gideal quantifies non‑ideality; models such as Margules, van Laar, Wilson, and NRTL provide analytical expressions for GE from which activity coefficients are derived by differentiation. In examinations, you may be asked to compute the activity of a component from a given excess‑Gibbs‑energy expression, or to verify the Gibbs‑Duhem relation for a binary mixture. Remember that the standard state for a solute in a liquid solution is usually the hypothetical 1 mol kg⁻¹ (or 1 M) ideal solution, not the pure liquid.

  • Assuming ΔH and ΔS are temperature‑independent when ΔCp is clearly non‑zero.
  • Confusing standard entropy S° (absolute) with standard enthalpy of formation ΔHf° (relative) and trying to apply a “formation” convention to entropy.
  • Forgetting that pure solids and liquids have unit activity and omitting them from Q, then incorrectly including them in the reaction quotient.
  • Using concentrations directly in the Nernst equation without converting to activities when ionic strength is high.
  • Mixing sign conventions: writing ΔG = +nFE instead of ΔG = −nFE, or treating a positive E° as non‑spontaneous.
  • Neglecting the temperature dependence of K when applying ΔG° = −RT ln K at a temperature different from the one at which K was given.
  • Treating partial molar quantities as simple molar quantities of the pure component, ignoring the Gibbs‑Duhem constraint.

hand/toric-varieties.html:
Cox Rings, Total Coordinate Rings, and GIT Quotients

The Cox ring of a toric variety X(Δ) is the polynomial ring ℂ[x_ρ : ρ ∈ Δ(1)] graded by the divisor class group Cl(X). Each variable x_ρ corresponds to the T‑invariant prime divisor D_ρ. The grading is given by deg(x_ρ) = [D_ρ] ∈ Cl(X). The irrelevant ideal B(Δ) is generated by monomials ∏ρ∉σ(1) x_ρ for each cone σ ∈ Δ. The toric variety is recovered as the GIT quotient (Spec Cox(X) V(B(Δ))) // Hom(Cl(X), ℂ^*), where the torus Hom(Cl(X), ℂ^*) acts with weights given by the grading. This construction generalises the classical description of projective space as (ℂn+1{0})/ℂ^* and of weighted projective spaces as quotients by a torus with non‑standard weights. The Cox ring is finitely generated precisely when X is a Mori dream space; for smooth complete toric varieties this always holds. The total coordinate ring provides a homogeneous coordinate system that makes many geometric questions — such as the computation of section rings of line bundles, the description of the movable cone, and the behaviour of the minimal model program — into combinatorial problems on the fan. In particular, the nef cone is the set of divisor classes whose representatives have non‑negative degree on all curves, and the effective cone is generated by the classes of the invariant divisors D_ρ. The Mori chamber decomposition of the effective cone corresponds to the different GIT quotients obtained by varying the stability condition, i.e. by choosing different characters of Hom(Cl(X), ℂ^*). Each chamber yields a birational model of X, and the walls correspond to flips or divisorial contractions in the minimal model program. This dictionary makes toric varieties a testing ground for the birational geometry of higher‑dimensional varieties.

Klyachko's Classification of Toric Vector Bundles

A toric vector bundle on X(Δ) is a vector bundle equipped with a T‑action lifting the action on the base. Klyachko showed that such bundles are equivalent to collections of finite decreasing filtrations of a fixed vector space E indexed by the rays of the fan, satisfying a compatibility condition. Concretely, for each ray ρ ∈ Δ(1) one assigns a filtration E = E^ρ(0) ⊇ E^ρ(1) ⊇ … ⊇ E^ρ(k_ρ) = 0 by subspaces. For any cone σ ∈ Δ, the intersection of the subspaces E^ρ(i_ρ) over ρ ∈ σ(1) must have dimension equal to the rank of the bundle minus the sum of the i_ρ. This condition ensures that the filtrations glue to a locally free sheaf. The classification reduces the study of toric vector bundles to linear algebra on the fan. Chern classes can be read off from the filtrations: the first Chern class is Σ_ρ (dim E - dim E^ρ(1)) D_ρ, and higher Chern classes are expressed as polynomials in the dimensions of the filtration steps. Stability of toric bundles with respect to a polarisation translates into numerical inequalities on the filtration dimensions, allowing a combinatorial check of (semi)stability. Moduli spaces of stable toric bundles are then described as GIT quotients of spaces of filtrations, and their geometry can be studied via the associated quiver representations. This framework has been used to construct examples of stable bundles with prescribed Chern classes, to compute cohomology via the Borel–Weil–Bott theorem for toric varieties, and to relate toric bundles to representations of the associated quiver with relations coming from the fan.

Worked Example: Filtrations for the Tangent Bundle of ℙ²
Let X = ℙ² with fan Δ having rays ρ₁, ρ₂, ρ₃ generated by (1,0), (0,1), (−1,−1). The tangent bundle T_X is a toric vector bundle of rank 2. Determine the Klyachko filtrations for each ray.
For ℙ² the divisor class group is ℤ, generated by the class of a line. The tangent bundle fits into the Euler sequence 0 → O → O(1)⊕3 → T_X → 0. The fibre of T_X at the fixed point corresponding to the cone σ = ⟨ρ₁,ρ₂⟩ is the weight space of the torus action on the tangent space. The T‑weights on the fibre are the characters χm where m runs over the primitive generators of the rays not in σ, i.e. m = (−1,−1). Thus the filtration for ρ₃ has a one‑dimensional step at level 1, while for ρ₁ and ρ₂ the filtrations are trivial (only the zero step). Explicitly: E = ℂ². For ρ₁: Eρ₁(0)=ℂ², Eρ₁(1)=0. For ρ₂: same. For ρ₃: Eρ₃(0)=ℂ², Eρ₃(1)=ℂ·e₁ (a line), Eρ₃(2)=0. The compatibility condition holds because for the cone ⟨ρ₁,ρ₂⟩ the intersection of the level‑1 subspaces is 0, matching rank 2 − (1+1)=0. This recovers the known splitting T_ℙ² ≅ O(1)⊕O(1) on the affine chart Uρ₁,ρ₂.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the Klyachko data of a standard bundle (tangent, cotangent, line bundles), first write the Euler sequence or the defining exact sequence. Identify the torus weights on the fibres at each fixed point; these give the filtration jumps. Remember that for a line bundle O(D) the filtration on ray ρ has a single jump at level equal to the coefficient of D_ρ in D. Practice converting between filtrations and the associated piecewise‑linear support function on the fan.

Tropical Geometry and Toric Degenerations

Tropical geometry provides a combinatorial shadow of algebraic geometry over the valuation field ℂ((t)). Given a subvariety Y ⊂ (ℂ^*)^n defined by Laurent polynomials, its tropicalisation Trop(Y) is a polyhedral complex in ℝ^n obtained by taking the valuation of the coordinates of points in Y. When Y is a hypersurface defined by a polynomial with Newton polytope P, Trop(Y) is the corner locus of the piecewise‑linear function given by the tropical polynomial, which is dual to a regular subdivision of P. Toric degenerations arise by considering a one‑parameter family X_t ⊂ X(Δ) where the defining equations are multiplied by powers of t according to a weight vector w ∈ ℝ^r. The central fibre X0 is a union of toric varieties glued along toric strata, and its dual intersection complex is homeomorphic to the tropical variety. This construction underlies the Gross–Siebert program for mirror symmetry: a Calabi‑Yau variety can be degenerated to a union of toric pieces whose dual complex carries an integral affine structure, and the mirror is reconstructed from the same data. In practice, one starts with a reflexive polytope P, chooses a regular triangulation of its polar P°, and obtains a toric degeneration of the Batyrev mirror Calabi‑Yau hypersurface. The tropical approach also gives a combinatorial formula for Gromov–Witten invariants via counts of tropical curves, which are piecewise‑linear graphs in ℝ^n satisfying a balancing condition at vertices. These counts match the algebraic counts after appropriate multiplicities are assigned, providing a powerful computational tool for enumerative geometry on toric varieties.

Equivariant Intersection Theory and Localization on Toric Varieties

The torus T = (ℂ^*)^n acts on X(Δ) with finitely many fixed points, one for each maximal cone σ ∈ Δ(n). The equivariant Chow ring A_T^*(X) is a module over the polynomial ring ℤ[λ₁,…,λ_n] = Sym(M), where λ_i are the characters of the standard basis of the torus. The localisation theorem states that the inclusion of the fixed point set i: X^T → X induces an injection i^*: A_T^*(X) ⊗ ℚ(λ) → A_T^*(X^T) ⊗ ℚ(λ) after inverting the equivariant parameters. Since X^T is a disjoint union of points, A_T^*(X^T) ≅ ⊕σ∈Δ(n) ℤ[λ]. The image of a class α ∈ A_T^*(X) is determined by its restrictions α|_σ, which are polynomials in λ. For an invariant divisor D_ρ, the restriction to the fixed point corresponding to σ is ⟨u_ρ, v_σ⟩ where u_ρ is the primitive generator of ρ and v_σ is the dual basis vector. This gives an explicit formula for the equivariant first Chern class of any line bundle. The ordinary Chow ring is recovered by setting the equivariant parameters to zero, i.e. by taking the quotient by the ideal generated by positive‑degree elements of ℤ[λ]. The localisation formula for integrals ∫_X α = Σσ α|_σ / e_T(N_σ) where e_T(N_σ) is the equivariant Euler class of the normal bundle at the fixed point, reduces intersection numbers to rational functions in λ that can be evaluated by taking the constant term. This technique yields closed formulas for Gromov–Witten invariants of toric varieties via the virtual localisation formula of Graber–Pandharipande, and it underlies the computation of quantum cohomology rings of toric Fano varieties.

Toric Mori Theory and the Minimal Model Program

The minimal model program (MMP) for toric varieties is completely governed by the combinatorics of the fan. A toric variety X(Δ) is ℚ‑factorial iff every cone of Δ is simplicial. The cone of curves NE(X) is generated by the classes of invariant curves C(τ) corresponding to codimension‑2 cones τ ∈ Δ(n−1). The intersection pairing with an invariant divisor D = Σ a_ρ D_ρ is D·C(τ) = Σρ∋τ a_ρ − Σρ∉τ, ρ∈σ a_ρ where σ is any maximal cone containing τ; this simplifies to a linear function on the coefficients a_ρ. The nef cone is the set of divisor classes with non‑negative intersection against all curves, and the ample cone is its interior. A K‑negative extremal ray R ⊂ NE(X) corresponds to a wall of the nef cone; the associated contraction morphism is either a divisorial contraction (blowing down a divisor to a lower‑dimensional toric stratum), a flip (replacing a curve by another curve in a different toric model), or a Mori fibre space structure (a toric fibration with relative Picard number one). All these operations have explicit fan descriptions: a divisorial contraction removes a ray from the fan, a flip replaces a ray by another ray in the same linear span, and a Mori fibre space corresponds to a projection of the fan onto a lower‑dimensional lattice. The toric MMP terminates because the number of rays strictly decreases in a divisorial contraction and the volume of the polytope associated to an ample divisor increases in a flip. This combinatorial termination proof was one of the first complete proofs of the MMP in any dimension. Moreover, the Cox ring provides a global description: the Mori chamber decomposition of the effective cone coincides with the GIT chambers for the action of Hom(Cl(X), ℂ^*) on Spec Cox(X), and each chamber corresponds to a birational model appearing in the MMP. This makes toric varieties the canonical laboratory for testing conjectures in higher‑dimensional birational geometry.

  • Confusing the Cox ring grading by Cl(X) with the grading by Pic(X); they coincide only when X is ℚ‑factorial.
  • Assuming every toric vector bundle splits as a sum of line bundles; this holds only on ℙⁿ and on certain Hirzebruch surfaces.
  • Misapplying the tropical balancing condition by forgetting the lattice length multiplicities on edges.
  • Using the localisation formula without inverting the equivariant parameters, leading to division by zero in the Euler class.
  • Thinking that every extremal contraction in the toric MMP is a divisorial contraction; flips occur whenever the contracted curve is not a toric divisor.
  • Neglecting the condition that the fan must be simplicial for ℚ‑factoriality, which is required for the cone of curves to be generated by invariant curves.
  • Overlooking that the Ehrhart polynomial counts lattice points in dilates of a polytope only for sufficiently large dilation; the formula fails for small t.

These advanced topics illustrate how the combinatorial data of fans and polytopes control the full birational and enumerative geometry of toric varieties.

hand/quantum-groups.html:
Drinfeld's Quantum Double: Construction and Universal R-Matrix

For a finite‑dimensional Hopf algebra H with multiplication m, comultiplication Δ, unit η, counit ε and antipode S, Drinfeld's quantum double D(H) is the vector space H*cop ⊗ H equipped with a Hopf algebra structure that makes it quasitriangular. The superscript cop denotes the opposite comultiplication on the dual H*. The multiplication in D(H) is defined by the cross‑relation

(f ⊗ a)(g ⊗ b) = Σ f (a₁ ⋅ g ⋅ S⁻¹(a₃)) ⊗ a₂ b

where Δ²(a) = Σ a₁ ⊗ a₂ ⊗ a₃ (Sweedler notation) and the left/right actions of H on H* are (a ⋅ f)(x) = f(x a), (f ⋅ a)(x) = f(a x). The comultiplication is the tensor product of the individual comultiplications: ΔD(f ⊗ a) = Σ (f₁ ⊗ a₁) ⊗ (f₂ ⊗ a₂). The antipode is SD(f ⊗ a) = (S⁻¹(f) ⊗ S(a)) after identifying H*cop with H* via the opposite comultiplication.

The universal R‑matrix of D(H) is the canonical element

R = Σi ei ⊗ ei

where {ei} is a basis of H and {ei} the dual basis of H*. One verifies directly that R Δ(x) R⁻¹ = Δop(x) for all x ∈ D(H) and that R satisfies the quantum Yang‑Baxter equation R₁₂ R₁₃ R₂₃ = R₂₃ R₁₃ R₁₂. Consequently D(H) is a quasitriangular Hopf algebra; if H is finite‑dimensional, D(H) is also factorizable, meaning the map H* → H induced by R is an isomorphism.

A fundamental example is H = Uq(𝔟+), the positive Borel subalgebra of the quantum group Uq(𝔤). Drinfeld proved that D(Uq(𝔟+)) is isomorphic to the full quantum group Uq(𝔤) as a Hopf algebra. Under this isomorphism the universal R‑matrix of Uq(𝔤) coincides with the canonical element of the double. This construction explains why every finite‑dimensional Hopf algebra yields a braided monoidal category of representations and provides a systematic source of solutions to the Yang‑Baxter equation.

Lusztig's Braid Group Action and the Quantum Weyl Group

Let Uq(𝔤) be the quantized universal enveloping algebra of a symmetrizable Kac‑Moody algebra with simple roots αi and simple reflections si of the Weyl group W. Lusztig constructed algebra automorphisms Ti : Uq(𝔤) → Uq(𝔤) for each simple index i that satisfy the braid relations

Ti Tj Ti ⋯ = Tj Ti Tj ⋯ (with mij factors on each side)

where mij is the order of si sj in W. The automorphisms are defined on the Chevalley generators by

Ti(Ei) = −Fi Ki, Ti(Fi) = −Ki⁻¹ Ei, Ti(Kj) = Kj Ki⁻aji

and for j ≠ i

Ti(Ej) = Σk=0−aij (−1)k qi−k Ei(−aij)−k Ej Ei(k)

with a similar formula for Fj. Here Ei(k) = Eik / [k]qi! are the divided powers. The maps Ti generate an action of the braid group BW on Uq(𝔤); this action is called the quantum Weyl group. It lifts the classical Weyl group action on the weight lattice and provides a powerful tool for moving between different highest‑weight modules.

The quantum Weyl group intertwines the coproduct: Δ ∘ Ti = (Ti ⊗ Ti) ∘ Δ. Consequently it induces equivalences of tensor categories of representations. Lusztig used these automorphisms to construct the canonical basis (also called the global crystal basis) of Uq(𝔤) and its representations. The basis elements are characterized by their invariance under a certain bar involution and by triangularity with respect to the PBW basis ordered by the quantum Weyl group action. This construction yields positivity of structure constants and underlies the categorification of quantum groups via perverse sheaves on quiver varieties.

Technique: Computing the action of Ti on generators of Uq(𝔰𝔩2)
Show that for Uq(𝔰𝔩2) with generators E, F, K±1 the Lusztig automorphism T satisfies T(E) = −F K, T(F) = −K⁻¹ E, and T(K) = K⁻¹.
In Uq(𝔰𝔩2) there is a single simple root, so the Cartan matrix entry a11 = 2. The general formula for Ti on the simple generators gives directly T(E) = −F K and T(F) = −K⁻¹ E. For the Cartan generator we use Ti(Kj) = Kj Ki⁻aji. With i = j = 1 and a11 = 2 we obtain T(K) = K K⁻² = K⁻¹. One checks that these assignments preserve the defining relations: K E K⁻¹ = q² E becomes K⁻¹ (−F K) K = −K⁻¹ F K² = q² (−F K) after using K F = q⁻² F K, which holds. Similarly the relation [E, F] = (K − K⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹) is preserved because T is an algebra automorphism by construction. Hence the formulas are correct.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the explicit action of Ti on the Chevalley generators and the braid relations. Questions often ask to verify that a given map defines a braid group action or to compute the image of a monomial under Ti. Knowing the divided‑power version of the formula for non‑simple generators saves time in proof‑based problems.

Crystal Bases and Canonical Bases: Combinatorial Structure of Representations

Kashiwara introduced crystal bases for integrable highest‑weight modules of Uq(𝔤) at q = 0. A crystal basis of a module V is a pair (L, B) where L is a free ℤ[q]-submodule of V stable under the Kashiwara operators ẽi, f̃i (the limits of the divided powers Ei(n), Fi(n) as q → 0) and B is a basis of the ℚ-vector space L / qL such that ẽi and f̃i act as partial maps on B sending basis elements to basis elements or zero. The directed graph with vertices B and coloured edges b → f̃i(b) is called the crystal graph. It encodes the weight decomposition and the action of the quantum group in a purely combinatorial way.

Lusztig's canonical basis (or global crystal basis) is a basis {bλ} of each irreducible highest‑weight module V(λ) defined over ℤ[q, q⁻¹] that specializes at q = 0 to the crystal basis. It is characterized by two properties: (1) invariance under the bar involution ¯ : Uq(𝔤) → Uq(𝔤) sending q q⁻¹ and fixing the Chevalley generators; (2) triangularity with respect to the PBW basis ordered by the quantum Weyl group action. The transition matrix between the canonical basis and any PBW basis is unitriangular with coefficients in ℕ[q, q⁻¹]. This positivity is a hallmark of the canonical basis and underlies its applications to total positivity and cluster algebras.

Crystal bases behave functorially with respect to tensor products: the crystal graph of V ⊗ W is the tensor product of the crystal graphs of V and W with the Kashiwara tensor product rule. This yields the Littlemann path model and the Kashiwara–Nakashima description of crystals for classical types. In type An the crystal graph of the fundamental representation is the set of semi‑standard Young tableaux, and the tensor product rule reproduces the Littlewood–Richardson rule. Thus crystal bases provide a combinatorial skeleton for the representation theory of quantum groups that survives the classical limit q → 1 and extends to affine and Borcherds algebras.

Quantum Groups at Roots of Unity and Modular Tensor Categories

When the deformation parameter q is a primitive ℓ‑th root of unity with ℓ odd and coprime to the determinant of the Cartan matrix, the representation theory of Uq(𝔤) changes dramatically. The algebra is no longer semisimple; there exist finite‑dimensional modules that are not completely reducible. However, by restricting to the subcategory of tilting modules and quotienting by the ideal of negligible morphisms (those with quantum trace zero), one obtains a semisimple braided tensor category Cℓ(𝔤). This category is a modular tensor category (MTC): it has finitely many simple objects, a non‑degenerate braiding, a ribbon twist, and a modular S‑matrix.

The simple objects of Cℓ(𝔤) are labelled by dominant weights λ lying in the alcove ⟨λ + ρ, θ⟩ ≤ ℓ − h∨, where θ is the highest root and h∨ the dual Coxeter number. The quantum dimensions dimq V(λ) are given by the Weyl denominator formula evaluated at the root of unity and are non‑zero precisely for these weights. The S‑matrix entries are

Sλ μ = (𝒟)⁻¹ᐟ² Σw ∈ W det(w) exp(2πi ⟨w(λ+ρ), μ+ρ⟩ / ℓ)

with 𝒟 = Σλ (dimq V(λ))². The Verlinde formula Nλ μν = Σσ Sλ σ Sμ σ Sν σ* / S0 σ computes the fusion coefficients (multiplicities in the tensor product of simple objects). The ribbon twist θλ = exp(2πi (⟨λ, λ+2ρ⟩ / 2ℓ)) gives the topological spin.

These MTCs are the algebraic input for the Reshetikhin–Turaev construction of 3‑manifold invariants and for topological quantum computation. In particular, the category Ck(𝔰𝔩2) at level k = ℓ − 2 yields the Fibonacci anyon when k = 3 (or equivalently ℓ = 5): the simple object with spin j = 1 has quantum dimension the golden ratio φ = (1+√5)/2 and its braiding generates a dense subgroup of SU(2), enabling universal quantum computation. The same categories appear as the representation categories of the Virasoro minimal models and of the Wess–Zumino–Witten conformal field theories, realizing the quantum group / CFT correspondence.

Quantum Affine Algebras and the Quantum Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov Equations

The quantum affine algebra Uq(ĝ) is the quantization of the universal enveloping algebra of the affine Kac–Moody algebra ĝ. Drinfeld gave two realizations: the loop presentation with generators Ei, Fi, Ki±¹ (i = 0,…,r) and the new realization in terms of Drinfeld currents Xi±(z), Φi±(z) satisfying certain commutation relations. The universal R‑matrix of Uq(ĝ) lives in a completion of Uq(ĝ) ⊗ Uq(ĝ) and satisfies the quantum Yang–Baxter equation with spectral parameters.

From the universal R‑matrix one constructs intertwiners Φλ(z) : V(λ) → V(λ) ⊗ V(z) where V(z) is an evaluation module. The matrix elements of products of intertwiners satisfy a system of linear difference equations known as the quantum Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov (qKZ) equations:

Φ(…, zi q2, …) = Ki(z1,…,zn) Φ(…, zi, …)

where the operators Ki are built from the R‑matrices Rij(zi/zj). These equations govern correlation functions in integrable lattice models (e.g. the XXZ spin chain) and in conformal field theory. Their solutions can be expressed as traces of intertwiners over highest‑weight modules, giving integral formulas (Jackson integrals) that generalize the classical KZ hypergeometric solutions.

The qKZ equations are closely related to the dynamical Yang–Baxter equation and to the representation theory of the elliptic quantum group Eτ,η(𝔰𝔩2). They also appear in the geometric Langlands program via the categorical action of the affine Hecke algebra on categories of D‑modules. For exam purposes, the key points are: (1) the definition of Uq(ĝ) via Drinfeld currents; (2) the construction of the universal R‑matrix with spectral parameter; (3) the derivation of the qKZ equations from the exchange relations of intertwiners; (4) the fact that at q = 1 the qKZ equations reduce to the classical KZ equations of conformal field theory.

  • Confusing the quantum double D(H) with the Drinfeld double of a Lie bialgebra; the former is a Hopf algebra construction, the latter is a classical limit.
  • Assuming the Lusztig automorphisms Ti are involutions; they satisfy braid relations but Ti² ≠ Id in general.
  • Treating crystal bases as ordinary bases at q = 1; they exist only at q = 0 and require the Kashiwara operators.
  • Forgetting that the modular tensor category at a root of unity is obtained after quotienting by negligible morphisms, not directly from the full representation category.
  • Misapplying the Verlinde formula outside the modular setting; it requires a non‑degenerate S‑matrix.
  • Overlooking the spectral parameter in the universal R‑matrix of Uq(ĝ); the qKZ equations depend crucially on this parameter.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the loop and new realizations of quantum affine algebras; exam questions often test the equivalence of the two presentations.

hand/symplectic-geometry.html:
Symplectic Capacities and the Non‑Squeezing Theorem

A symplectic capacity is a function c that assigns to each symplectic manifold (M,ω) a number in [0,∞] satisfying three axioms: monotonicity (if there exists a symplectic embedding φ: (M₁,ω₁) → (M₂,ω₂) then c(M₁) ≤ c(M₂)), conformality (c(M,λω) = λ c(M,ω) for λ>0), and normalization (c(B²ⁿ(r)) = c(Z²ⁿ(r)) = π r² where B²ⁿ(r) is the standard ball and Z²ⁿ(r) = B²(r) × ℝ²ⁿ⁻² the cylinder). The first non‑trivial capacity was discovered by Gromov in 1985: the Gromov width w_G(M) = sup{π r² | B²ⁿ(r) symplectically embeds into M}. Gromov’s non‑squeezing theorem states that a ball B²ⁿ(R) cannot be symplectically embedded into a cylinder Z²ⁿ(r) unless R ≤ r. This result shows that symplectic geometry has a rigidity absent in volume‑preserving diffeomorphisms (which can squeeze a ball arbitrarily thin). Subsequent capacities include the Hofer–Zehnder capacity c_HZ, defined via Hamiltonian dynamics on the manifold, and the Ekeland–Hofer capacities c_k obtained from the minimax principle on the loop space. These capacities give sharp obstructions to embeddings: for example, the sequence c_k(ℝ²ⁿ) = kπ distinguishes symplectic ellipsoids E(a₁,…,aₙ) up to symplectomorphism. The symplectic camel phenomenon (a ball can pass through a hole in a hypersurface only if the hole’s capacity is at least that of the ball) illustrates the global nature of these invariants. Capacities also play a role in Hamiltonian dynamics: c_HZ(M) > 0 implies the existence of periodic orbits on energy surfaces (the Weinstein conjecture for certain contact type hypersurfaces). Computing capacities for specific manifolds — such as polydiscs, ellipsoids, and toric domains — remains an active area, with recent progress using embedded contact homology and J‑holomorphic curves.

Contact Geometry, Symplectization, and the Weinstein Conjecture

A contact manifold (Y,ξ) of dimension 2n−1 is a hyperplane field ξ = ker α defined by a 1‑form α with α ∧ (dα)ⁿ⁻¹ ≠ 0. The Reeb vector field R_α is uniquely determined by α(R_α)=1 and dα(R_α,·)=0. Every contact manifold admits a symplectization (ℝ × Y, d(e^t α)), which is an exact symplectic manifold carrying a Liouville vector field ∂_t. Conversely, a hypersurface of contact type in a symplectic manifold inherits a contact structure. The Weinstein conjecture (1978) asserts that every closed contact manifold carries a closed Reeb orbit. In dimension three, Taubes proved the conjecture in 2007 using Seiberg–Witten theory and embedded contact homology (ECH). Higher‑dimensional cases remain open in general, but are known for many classes: overtwisted contact manifolds (by Eliashberg), dynamically convex contact spheres (by Hofer–Wysocki–Zehnder), and contact manifolds admitting a Liouville filling with vanishing symplectic homology. The contact homology of Eliashberg–Givental–Hofer, built from Reeb orbits and pseudoholomorphic curves in the symplectization, provides a powerful invariant that distinguishes contact structures. The Legendrian knot theory studies submanifolds L ⊂ Y tangent to ξ; their Chekanov–Eliashberg differential graded algebra is an invariant derived from counting pseudoholomorphic disks with boundary on ℝ × L. Recent work on flexible vs. rigid Legendrians (Murphy–Cieliebak–Eliashberg) shows that the h‑principle holds for loose Legendrians, while tight ones carry subtle symplectic invariants. Contact geometry also underlies the convex integration techniques used to construct symplectic embeddings and to prove the existence of exotic symplectic structures on ℝ⁴.

Worked Example: Computing the Gromov Width of an Ellipsoid
Let E(a,b) = { (z₁,z₂) ∈ ℂ² | π|z₁|²/a + π|z₂|²/b < 1 } with 0 < a ≤ b. Determine the Gromov width w_G(E(a,b)).
The Gromov width of a symplectic manifold is the supremum of π r² such that a ball B⁴(r) embeds symplectically. For an ellipsoid E(a,b), the optimal embedding of a ball is given by the Ekeland–Hofer capacities c_k(E(a,b)). The first capacity c₁(E(a,b)) = a (since a ≤ b). By monotonicity and normalization, any ball B⁴(r) embedded in E(a,b) must satisfy π r² ≤ c₁(E(a,b)) = a. Conversely, the inclusion B⁴(√(a/π)) → E(a,b) given by (z₁,z₂) ↦ (z₁, z₂) is symplectic because the ball’s defining inequality π|z₁|² + π|z₂|² < a implies the ellipsoid inequality. Hence the supremum is attained and w_G(E(a,b)) = a.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a symplectic embedding obstruction, first identify the relevant capacity (Gromov width, Hofer–Zehnder, or Ekeland–Hofer). Compute the first few capacities of the target domain using known formulas for ellipsoids, polydiscs, or toric domains. Then apply monotonicity: the capacity of the source cannot exceed that of the target. Remember that capacities are invariant under symplectomorphisms but not under mere diffeomorphisms; always check the symplectic form scaling.

Geometric Quantization and Deformation Quantization

Geometric quantization constructs a Hilbert space from a symplectic manifold (M,ω) with integral symplectic form [ω/2π] ∈ H²(M;ℤ). One chooses a prequantum line bundle L → M with connection of curvature −i ω. The prequantum Hilbert space consists of square‑integrable sections of L. To halve the degrees of freedom one selects a polarization — a Lagrangian distribution integrable to a foliation (real polarization) or a complex structure (Kähler polarization). For a Kähler manifold, the quantum Hilbert space is the space of holomorphic sections H⁰(M,L). The metaplectic correction (tensoring with the half‑form bundle) resolves anomalies and yields the correct semiclassical limit. Deformation quantization, initiated by Bayen–Flato–Fronsdal–Lichnerowicz–Sternheimer (1978), seeks an associative star product f ★ g = fg + (iħ/2){f,g} + O(ħ²) on C^∞(M)[[ħ]] deforming the Poisson algebra. Kontsevich’s formality theorem (1997) proves that every Poisson manifold admits a star product, constructed via graphs and the Kontsevich integral. For symplectic manifolds, the Fedosov construction (1994) gives a canonical star product using a symplectic connection and Weyl curvature. The characteristic class of a star product lives in H²(M)[[ħ]] and classifies equivalence classes. The index theorem for deformation quantization (Nest–Tsygan) relates the trace functional on the deformed algebra to the Todd class of M. Both quantization schemes converge in the semiclassical limit: the Berezin–Toeplitz quantization on Kähler manifolds produces a star product whose asymptotic expansion matches the geometric quantization data. Recent developments include quantization of symplectic groupoids (Weinstein, Xu) and the role of derived algebraic geometry in the quantization of shifted symplectic structures (Pantev–Toën–Vaquié–Vezzosi).

Lagrangian Intersection Theory and the Arnold Conjecture Revisited

The Arnold conjecture (1965) predicts that a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism φ_H¹ of a closed symplectic manifold (M,ω) has at least as many fixed points as the sum of Betti numbers ∑ dim H^k(M;ℚ) (or the cup‑length plus one for non‑degenerate fixed points). Floer’s original proof (1988) for monotone symplectic manifolds used the Floer homology HF_*(H) of a non‑degenerate Hamiltonian H, defined as the homology of a chain complex generated by 1‑periodic Hamiltonian orbits with differential counting pseudoholomorphic cylinders. The PSS isomorphism (Piunikhin–Salamon–Schwarz, 1996) identifies HF_*(H) with the quantum homology QH_*(M), which as a vector space equals H_*(M) ⊗ Λ (Novikov ring). This yields the lower bound #Fix(φ_H¹) ≥ rank QH_*(M) = ∑ dim H^k(M). For general symplectic manifolds, the conjecture was settled by Ono (1995) using virtual fundamental cycles and by Fukaya–Ono (1999) via Kuranishi structures. The Lagrangian Arnold conjecture concerns intersections of a Lagrangian L with its Hamiltonian image φ_H¹(L); Floer homology HF_*(L, φ_H¹(L)) gives a lower bound by the sum of Betti numbers of L (when L is relatively spin and monotone). The Oh spectral sequence relates Lagrangian Floer homology to singular homology of L. Recent advances include wrapped Floer homology for non‑compact Lagrangians (Abouzaid–Seidel) and the sheaf‑theoretic approach (Nadler–Zaslow, Guillermou–Kashiwara–Schapira) which identifies the Fukaya category with constructible sheaves on the Lagrangian skeleton. The Arnold–Givental conjecture on the existence of a generating function quadratic at infinity for Lagrangian submanifolds of T*ℝⁿ was proved by Viterbo (1992) using symplectic homology. These results illustrate how pseudoholomorphic curve techniques translate dynamical questions into algebraic topology.

Integrable Systems, Action‑Angle Variables, and the Liouville‑Arnold Theorem

A Hamiltonian system on a 2n-dimensional symplectic manifold (M,ω) is completely integrable if there exist n independent functions F₁,…,Fₙ ∈ C^∞(M) in involution ({F_i,F_j}=0) such that the Hamiltonian H is a function of them. The Liouville–Arnold theorem states that if the common level set Λ_c = {F₁=c₁,…,Fₙ=cₙ} is compact and connected, then it is a Lagrangian torus Tⁿ and there exists a neighbourhood symplectomorphic to Tⁿ × Bⁿ with coordinates (θ₁,…,θₙ, I₁,…,Iₙ) (action‑angle variables) where ω = Σ dI_i ∧ dθ_i and the Hamiltonian depends only on the actions I. The flows are linear on the tori: θ_i(t) = θ_i(0) + ω_i(I) t with frequencies ω_i = ∂H/∂I_i. The monodromy of the action variables around singular fibres (e.g., focus‑focus singularities) is a topological obstruction to global action‑angle coordinates; it is measured by the non‑triviality of the torus bundle over the base of the Lagrangian fibration. The KAM theorem (Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser) asserts that for a non‑degenerate integrable Hamiltonian, most invariant tori survive under small perturbations, preserving quasi‑periodic motion. In the symplectic setting, symplectic topology of integrable systems studies the classification of Lagrangian fibrations up to symplectomorphism; the Duistermaat–Heckman formula computes the pushforward of the Liouville measure under the moment map, yielding piecewise polynomial densities. Quantum integrable systems correspond to commuting quantum Hamiltonians; their joint spectrum exhibits lattice structures approximated by the Bohr–Sommerfeld conditions ∮γ_i p dq = 2πħ (k_i + μ_i/4) where μ_i are Maslov indices. The semi‑classical trace formula (Gutzwiller) expresses the density of states as a sum over periodic orbits, linking classical integrability to quantum spectral statistics. Modern work on cluster integrable systems (Fock–Goncharov) connects Poisson structures on moduli spaces of local systems to symplectic geometry of cluster varieties.

  • Confusing symplectic capacity with volume — capacities are symplectic invariants, volume is not.
  • Assuming every contact manifold satisfies the Weinstein conjecture without checking dimension or known results.
  • Neglecting the integrality condition [ω/2π] ∈ H²(M;ℤ) when setting up geometric quantization.
  • Applying the Arnold conjecture lower bound to degenerate Hamiltonians without perturbing to non‑degenerate ones.
  • Overlooking monodromy when claiming global action‑angle coordinates exist for an integrable system.
  • Treating deformation quantization star products as unique; they are classified by characteristic classes.
  • Using the KAM theorem for degenerate frequency maps — non‑degeneracy (twist condition) is essential.

hand/condensed-math.html:
Condensed Spectra and the Six‑Functor Formalism

The category of condensed spectra, denoted Sp(Cond), is the stable ∞‑category obtained by stabilizing the ∞‑category of condensed sets. It carries a symmetric monoidal structure given by the smash product of condensed spectra, and it admits a full six‑functor formalism for morphisms of condensed analytic spaces. For a morphism f : X → Y of condensed analytic spaces one has the adjoint pairs (f*, f*), (f!, f^!) and the internal tensor–Hom adjunction (⊗, Hom). The functors f* and f! are defined by left Kan extension along the underlying map of condensed sets, while f* and f^! are their right adjoints. The construction relies on the fact that condensed sets form a cohesive ∞‑topos, so the usual formalism of Grothendieck’s six operations for étale cohomology transfers verbatim after replacing sheaves of abelian groups by condensed spectra. A key theorem of Clausen–Scholze (2022) states that the derived category of solid modules D(Solid) embeds fully faithfully into Sp(Cond) as the subcategory of connective objects with respect to the natural t‑structure. This embedding identifies the solid six‑functor formalism with the restriction of the condensed one, and it shows that the pathologies of classical p‑adic functional analysis disappear: the sum of two closed submodules is closed, and the open mapping theorem holds for all morphisms of solid Banach spaces. The formalism also provides a natural home for the pro‑étale cohomology of perfectoid spaces, because the pro‑étale site of a perfectoid space is equivalent to the condensed site of its associated condensed analytic space.

Derived Analytic Geometry on the Pro‑étale Site

Derived analytic geometry replaces the structure sheaf of a rigid analytic space by a sheaf of E∞‑ring spectra on the pro‑étale site. In the condensed framework an analytic ring (A, A■) is a condensed ring equipped with a solid module structure that plays the role of a completion functor. The pro‑étale site of a perfectoid space X is equivalent to the site of condensed sets over the condensed analytic space X■, and the structure sheaf OX■ becomes a sheaf of analytic rings. The derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on X is then identified with the derived category of solid OX■‑modules. This identification yields a derived version of the almost purity theorem: for a perfectoid algebra R the natural map R → R■ induces an equivalence between the derived category of almost R‑modules and the derived category of solid R■‑modules. Consequently, the derived de Rham cohomology of a smooth rigid analytic variety can be computed as the condensed Hochschild homology of its analytic ring of functions. The formalism also clarifies the relationship between the v‑topology and the pro‑étale topology: a morphism of perfectoid spaces is a v‑cover if and only if it becomes an effective epimorphism in the condensed topos. This equivalence is the technical engine behind the Fargues–Scholze construction of the local Langlands correspondence, because it allows one to treat the stack of G‑bundles on the Fargues–Fontaine curve as a small v‑stack and to apply the six‑functor formalism to its ℓ‑adic cohomology.

Technique: Identifying the Compact‑Support Pushforward
Let f : X → Y be a morphism of condensed analytic spaces. Which of the six functors computes the derived pushforward with compact support, and what is its left adjoint?
The functor f_! is the derived pushforward with compact support. Its left adjoint is the exceptional pullback f^!. The adjunction (f_!, f^!) is part of the six‑functor formalism on Sp(Cond) and satisfies the usual base‑change and projection formulas. In particular, for a proper morphism f one has f_! ≅ f_*.
Exam Day Strategy
Memorise the six functor names (f*, f*, f!, f^!, ⊗, Hom) and their adjunction pairs. Draw a quick 2×3 table on scrap paper; it saves time when a question asks for the correct functor in a given adjunction.

Condensed Hochschild and Cyclic Homology for Analytic Rings

For an analytic ring (A, A■) the condensed Hochschild homology HH■(A) is defined as the derived tensor product A ⊗A⊗A■ A taken in the symmetric monoidal ∞‑category of solid A‑modules. The resulting object carries a natural circle action, and its homotopy fixed points give the condensed cyclic homology HC■(A). When A is the analytic ring of a smooth algebra over a characteristic‑zero field, the HKR theorem holds in the condensed setting: HH■(A) is equivalent to the derived de Rham complex ΩA■, and HC■(A) recovers the negative cyclic homology which computes algebraic de Rham cohomology. For a perfectoid ring R the condensed Hochschild homology specializes to the prismatic cohomology of Bhatt–Scholze; in particular, HH■(R)⊗ℤ ℤp carries a natural Frobenius and its derived completion yields the Nygaard filtration. This identification provides a unified approach to p‑adic Hodge theory: the filtered φ‑module associated to a proper smooth formal scheme over the ring of integers of a p‑adic field is obtained by applying the condensed cyclic homology functor to its analytic ring of functions and then taking the appropriate graded pieces. The formalism also explains the degeneration of the Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence in the condensed world, because the circle action on HH■ is automatically split after passing to solid modules.

Condensed Modules over Perfectoid Rings and Almost Mathematics

The almost mathematics of Faltings, developed to handle the torsion phenomena in p‑adic Hodge theory, finds a clean categorical formulation in condensed mathematics. Let R be a perfectoid ring with pseudo‑uniformizer ϖ. The category of almost R‑modules is the quotient of the category of R‑modules by the Serre subcategory of ϖ‑power torsion modules. Clausen–Scholze proved that the natural functor from almost R‑modules to solid R■‑modules is an equivalence of symmetric monoidal stable ∞‑categories. Under this equivalence the almost tensor product corresponds to the derived solid tensor product, and the almost Hom corresponds to the internal Hom in solid modules. The almost purity theorem — stating that a finite étale extension of perfectoid rings is almost finite étale — becomes the statement that the corresponding map of analytic rings is a solid‑étale cover, i.e. an effective epimorphism in the condensed topos that is locally a finite free solid module. This perspective eliminates the need for the cumbersome “almost” language in many proofs: one simply works in the category of solid modules where all limits and colimits exist and behave well. For example, the derived category of almost coherent sheaves on a perfectoid space is equivalent to the derived category of solid coherent sheaves on its condensed analytic space, and the six‑functor formalism for solid modules provides the correct pushforward and pullback functors without any almost‑ification steps.

The Condensed Geometric Satake Equivalence for the Fargues–Fontaine Curve

The geometric Satake equivalence in the condensed setting identifies the category of equivariant perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian GrG of a reductive group G over ℚp with the category of representations of the Langlands dual group Ǧ. In the Fargues–Scholze program the affine Grassmannian is realized as a condensed ind‑scheme, and the category of ℓ‑adic perverse sheaves on it is defined using the six‑functor formalism on condensed spectra. The key input is the condensed version of the Beilinson–Drinfeld Grassmannian, which allows one to construct the convolution product on perverse sheaves as a correspondence in the condensed topos. The resulting monoidal equivalence is compatible with the fiber functor given by the stalk at the base point, and it yields a Tannakian reconstruction of Ǧ. This equivalence is then used to construct the local Langlands correspondence for G(ℚp) by passing to the stack of G‑bundles BunG on the Fargues–Fontaine curve X. The stack BunG is a small v‑stack in the condensed sense, and its ℓ‑adic cohomology carries an action of the Weil group Wℚp. The Fargues–Scholze theorem states that the category of Weil representations of Wℚp is equivalent to the category of perverse sheaves on BunG that are Hecke‑eigensheaves with eigenvalues given by the Satake parameters. The condensed formalism is essential because BunG is infinite‑dimensional and not an algebraic stack in the classical sense; the condensed topos provides a setting where it becomes a geometric object with a well‑behaved six‑functor formalism.

  • Confusing the solid six‑functor formalism with the classical étale six‑functor formalism; they coincide only after embedding D(Solid) into Sp(Cond).
  • Assuming that the pro‑étale site of a perfectoid space is the same as its v‑site; they are equivalent as condensed topoi but have different covering families.
  • Misidentifying the functor that computes compact‑support pushforward; it is f_!, not f_*.
  • Thinking that condensed Hochschild homology always agrees with classical Hochschild homology; the condensed version incorporates the solid completion and can differ on non‑smooth algebras.
  • Believing that almost mathematics is a separate theory; in condensed language it is exactly the category of solid modules over a perfectoid analytic ring.
  • Overlooking that the geometric Satake equivalence in the condensed setting requires the affine Grassmannian to be treated as a condensed ind‑scheme, not as a classical ind‑scheme.
  • Neglecting the role of the circle action on condensed Hochschild homology; it is the source of the cyclic homology and the Nygaard filtration in p‑adic Hodge theory.
