hand/factorization-algebras.html:
Renormalization and the Heat Kernel in Factorization Algebras

The quantization of a factorization algebra is governed by the renormalization group flow, which in the Costello–Gwilliam framework is implemented through a family of effective actions parametrized by a length scale ℓ > 0. The heat kernel K_ℓ of the kinetic operator provides a canonical regulator: for a free theory with quadratic action ½⟨φ, Qφ⟩, the propagator at scale ℓ is the integral of the heat kernel from ℓ to ∞. This propagator defines a prefactorization algebra 𝒪_ℓ whose structure maps are given by sums over Feynman diagrams with edges labelled by the regulated propagator. As ℓ → 0 the diagrams diverge; the renormalization procedure consists of adding local counterterms — themselves elements of the space of local functionals — so that the limit exists in the homotopy category of prefactorization algebras. The key theorem states that the space of such renormalizations is a torsor for the group of local counterterms, and the anomaly (the obstruction to ℓ-independence) is measured by the quantum master equation ħΔS + ½{S, S} = 0. In practice, one computes the effective action S_ℓ by the recursive formula S_ℓ = W(P_ℓ, S) where W is the renormalization group operator built from the heat kernel and P_ℓ is the propagator at scale ℓ. The heat kernel asymptotics guarantee that counterterms are local polynomials in the fields and their derivatives, which matches the physical expectation that ultraviolet divergences are absorbed by redefining couplings in the Lagrangian. This construction works for any elliptic kinetic operator on a manifold, and the resulting quantum factorization algebra is independent of the choice of heat kernel up to canonical equivalence.

An important subtlety arises when the theory has gauge symmetries. The BV formalism extends the field space by antifields and ghosts, and the kinetic operator becomes the BV differential Q_BV. The heat kernel of Q_BV is then a homotopy operator for the BV complex, and the same renormalization group flow produces a quantum BV action satisfying the quantum master equation. The cohomology of the quantum BV differential (Q_BV + ħΔ) on the space of observables yields the algebra of quantum observables. In the holomorphic setting on a Riemann surface, the heat kernel of the ∂̄-operator is the Cauchy kernel, and the renormalization group flow reproduces the standard normal-ordering prescription of vertex algebras. Thus the heat kernel provides a unified geometric mechanism for renormalization across topological, holomorphic, and conformal factorization algebras.

Higher Genus Factorization Homology and Modular Invariance

Factorization homology ∫_M 𝒜 of a factorization algebra 𝒜 on a manifold M is defined by a colimit over the Ran space of M. For a two‑dimensional oriented surface Σ of genus g, the factorization homology of a holomorphic factorization algebra (equivalently a vertex algebra V) computes the space of conformal blocks of V on Σ. The sewing axioms of conformal field theory are encoded in the factorization property: cutting Σ along a separating circle corresponds to the factorization product in 𝒜, while cutting along a non‑separating circle corresponds to the trace (or “handle‑gluing”) operation. The modular group Sp(2g, ℤ) acts on the homology of Σ, and the resulting action on conformal blocks is the monodromy of the projectively flat connection on the bundle of conformal blocks over the moduli space ℳ_g. In the factorization algebra language, this connection is the Gauss–Manin connection on the factorization homology viewed as a sheaf on ℳ_g. The Verlinde formula, which expresses the dimension of the space of conformal blocks in terms of the modular S‑matrix of the vertex algebra, follows from the fact that factorization homology is a symmetric monoidal functor from the category of surfaces with boundaries to vector spaces. For a rational vertex algebra, the category of modules is a modular tensor category, and factorization homology recovers the Reshetikhin–Turaev topological quantum field theory. At higher genus, the factorization algebra must satisfy the “genus‑g locality” condition: the OPE of fields inserted on a genus‑g surface must be single‑valued under the action of the mapping class group. This condition is equivalent to the requirement that the vertex algebra be C₂‑cofinite and rational, which guarantees that the space of conformal blocks is finite‑dimensional and carries a projective representation of the mapping class group. The factorization homology perspective thus provides a conceptual proof of modular invariance: it is the statement that the symmetric monoidal functor ∫− 𝒜 extends from the category of disks to the whole oriented 2‑dimensional cobordism category.

Worked Example: Heat Kernel Counterterm for a Free Scalar
Consider a free scalar field φ on ℝ^d with action S = ½∫ φ(−Δ)φ. The heat kernel of −Δ is K_ℓ(x,y) = (4πℓ)-d/2 exp(−|x−y|²/4ℓ). Compute the one‑loop counterterm needed to cancel the ℓ → 0 divergence of the two‑point function at coincident points.
The regulated propagator is P_ℓ(x,y) = ∫_ℓ^∞ K_t(x,y) dt. At coincident points x=y, K_t(x,x) = (4πt)-d/2. The divergence as ℓ→0 is ∫_ℓ1 t-d/2 dt. For d=2 this gives −log ℓ, for d=4 it gives ℓ-1. The counterterm is a local functional ∫ c ℓ2−d φ² (or ∫ c log ℓ φ² in d=2) added to the action. In the BV language this corresponds to adding a term to the quantum action S_ℓ such that the quantum master equation holds order by order in ħ. The coefficient c is fixed by requiring that the limit of the effective two‑point function exists. This illustrates the general principle: heat kernel asymptotics determine the form of local counterterms.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the role of the heat kernel in renormalization, state explicitly that it provides a canonical propagator at scale ℓ, that its short‑time asymptotics produce local counterterms, and that the renormalization group flow is the map ℓ ↦ S_ℓ defined by the BV renormalization group operator. Mention the quantum master equation as the consistency condition. Avoid vague statements like “it regularizes divergences” without linking to the BV differential and the limit ℓ→0.

The Ran Space and Chiral Homology: Local-to-Global Principles

The Ran space Ran(X) of a smooth curve X is the ind‑scheme whose S‑points are non‑empty finite subsets of X(S). Its topology is the colimit of symmetric products X(n) with the natural maps given by adding diagonals. A chiral algebra 𝒜 on X is a 𝒟‑module on Ran(X) equipped with a factorization isomorphism 𝒜|Ran(X)×X Ran(X) ≅ 𝒜 ⊠ 𝒜 away from the diagonal, satisfying associativity and commutativity constraints. The chiral homology H_*(X, 𝒜) is defined as the factorization homology ∫_X 𝒜, i.e. the derived global sections of the 𝒟‑module 𝒜 on Ran(X) pushed forward to a point. The fundamental local‑to‑global principle states that the chiral algebra is completely determined by its restriction to the formal punctured disc D^×_x at each point x ∈ X, together with the factorization isomorphisms that glue these local data. This is the geometric analogue of the statement that a vertex algebra is determined by its state‑field correspondence and the OPE. The Beilinson–Drinfeld construction of the chiral algebra of an affine Kac–Moody algebra at level k proceeds by taking the 𝒟‑module of vacuum modules on the Ran space of the curve and imposing the factorization structure coming from the fusion of representations. The resulting chiral algebra is a 𝒟‑module on Ran(X) whose fiber at a finite set {x₁,…,x_n} is the space of conformal blocks of the affine algebra at those points. The KZ connection arises as the flat connection on this 𝒟‑module induced by the projective action of the mapping class group on conformal blocks. In the language of factorization algebras, the Ran space is the classifying space for the factorization structure, and chiral homology is the value of the factorization homology functor on the curve. This perspective makes it clear why the geometric Langlands correspondence involves 𝒟‑modules on Bun_G: the Hecke eigensheaf condition is precisely a factorization property with respect to the Ran space of the curve, and the eigenvalues are given by a local system on X, i.e. a point in the moduli of ^L G‑local systems.

Critical Level Affine Kac-Moody Algebras and the Feigin-Frenkel Isomorphism

For a simple Lie algebra 𝔤 with dual Coxeter number h^∨, the affine Kac–Moody algebra 𝔤̂ at level k = −h^∨ is called the critical level. At this level the Sugawara construction of the Virasoro algebra fails because the central charge vanishes, and the center of the completed universal enveloping algebra 𝔘̂(𝔤̂)crit becomes large. The Feigin–Frenkel theorem identifies this center Z(𝔤̂crit) with the algebra of functions on the space Op^L G(D) of ^L G‑opers on the formal disc D = Spec ℂ[[t]]. An ^L G‑oper is a ^L G‑bundle with a connection and a reduction to a Borel subgroup satisfying a transversality condition; the space of opers is an infinite‑dimensional affine space modeled on the space of differential operators of the form ∂^n + q₂∂n−2 + … + q_n. The isomorphism is constructed by the quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction: one takes the BRST complex of the affine algebra with respect to the nilpotent subalgebra, and the cohomology in degree zero yields the center. The generators of the center are the quantum Miura opers, which are explicit differential operators built from the currents of the affine algebra. This result has two major consequences. First, it provides a geometric realization of the center as functions on a space of opers, which are precisely the classical Hitchin Hamiltonians for the Langlands dual group. Second, it implies that any representation of 𝔤̂crit on which the center acts by a character corresponds to an ^L G‑oper, i.e. a point in the moduli of ^L G‑local systems. In the geometric Langlands program, Hecke eigensheaves on Bun_G are constructed by taking the chiral homology of the critical level affine algebra twisted by a local system; the Feigin–Frenkel isomorphism guarantees that the resulting 𝒟‑module has the correct eigenvalues. The critical level is also the level at which the affine vertex algebra admits a conformal structure with central charge zero, making it a natural object in the derived category of chiral algebras.

Elliptic Cohomology, Topological Modular Forms, and Factorization Algebras

Elliptic cohomology is a generalized cohomology theory whose coefficient ring is the ring of modular forms. The topological modular forms spectrum TMF is a connective version constructed by Goerss–Hopkins–Miller using the moduli stack ℳell of elliptic curves and a sheaf of E_∞ ring spectra 𝒪top. In the factorization algebra framework, TMF can be obtained as the factorization homology of a certain 2‑dimensional topological factorization algebra 𝒜ell over the moduli stack ℳell. The algebra 𝒜ell assigns to a disk the E_∞ algebra of functions on the derived moduli of elliptic curves with a chosen trivialization of the formal group, and its factorization product encodes the gluing of elliptic curves along boundary circles. The resulting factorization homology ∫ℳell 𝒜ell recovers the global sections of 𝒪top, i.e. TMF. This construction realizes the idea that elliptic cohomology is a “2‑dimensional topological field theory” valued in spectra. The connection to vertex algebras appears through the Witten genus: the partition function of a supersymmetric sigma model on an elliptic curve is a modular form, and the corresponding vertex algebra is the chiral de Rham complex of the target manifold. The factorization algebra of the chiral de Rham complex on a Riemann surface computes the elliptic genus, and its factorization homology over ℳell yields the TMF‑valued elliptic genus. Moreover, the derived moduli of elliptic curves carries a natural action of the mapping class group of the torus, which is SL₂(ℤ); the modularity of TMF is precisely the statement that the factorization algebra 𝒜ell is equivariant with respect to this action. This perspective unifies the appearance of modular forms in conformal field theory, the geometry of ℳell, and the homotopy theory of E_∞ ring spectra, showing that factorization algebras provide the natural language for “elliptic” objects across mathematics.

  • Confusing the heat kernel regulator with a generic cutoff; the heat kernel is canonical for elliptic operators and yields local counterterms, whereas a sharp momentum cutoff breaks locality.
  • Assuming factorization homology on a surface always equals the space of conformal blocks; this holds only for rational, C₂‑cofinite vertex algebras, otherwise the homology may be infinite‑dimensional or fail to carry a mapping class group action.
  • Treating the Ran space as an ordinary scheme; it is an ind‑scheme, and 𝒟‑modules on it must be understood in the ind‑pro‑category, otherwise factorization isomorphisms cannot be formulated correctly.
  • Stating that the Feigin–Frenkel isomorphism holds at any level; it is specific to the critical level k = −h^∨, where the center becomes the algebra of functions on opers.
  • Claiming TMF is the factorization homology of the chiral de Rham complex on a single elliptic curve; TMF requires factorization homology over the whole moduli stack ℳell, not just a fiber.
  • Neglecting the projective nature of the mapping class group action on conformal blocks; the action lifts to a linear action only after choosing a central extension, which is encoded in the factorization algebra by the anomaly term in the quantum master equation.
  • Overlooking that the quantum master equation ħΔS + ½{S, S} = 0 is a condition on the quantum action, not on the classical action alone; the classical master equation {S, S} = 0 is necessary but not sufficient for quantization.
